summary: This work theoretically investigates spatially localized quantum solitons in linear arrays of capacitively coupled transmons described by the attractive Bose-Hubbard model, and proposes protocols for their preparation and characterization via quantum walks in transmon circuits. The solitonic states are superpositions of the lowest-energy band eigenstates with exponentially localized density profiles, revealing composite-particle behavior distinct from both single-particle and boson-stack dynamics.
motivation: Quantum simulation with superconducting transmon arrays can realize the attractive Bose-Hubbard model, where strong correlations and particle clustering make classical simulation difficult; quantum walks of composite solitonic excitations provide both fundamental insight into quantum interference in interacting systems and potential applications in quantum-enhanced sensing.
method: Three protocols construct spatially localized quantum solitons from soliton-band eigenstates (projected boson stacks, single-stack solitons, narrowest solitons); for transmon implementation, a non-adiabatic protocol prepares solitons by evolving a boson stack under constant pinning $\Delta\mu_i \approx U(N-1)$ for time $t_0 \approx \pi/2|U|(N-1)$, then quenching to the uniform system. Fidelities exceed 99.8% for $N=2$ and 99.999% for $N\geq5$ with typical transmon parameters ($E_J/E_C \approx 50$–100, $J \approx 1$–40 MHz, $|U| \approx E_C/\hbar \sim$ hundreds of MHz).
result: Quantum walks of localized solitons ($U=-10J$, $N=2,3$) show composite-particle behavior with reduced high-momentum components compared to unprojected boson stacks; Hellinger distances between soliton and single-particle density distributions remain smaller than boson-stack distances at short timescales, and single-boson occupation at array edges reaches percent level only after times $\sim(M-1)/2\cdot2\tilde{J}$ compared to $\sim(M-1)/2J$ for uncorrelated particles, enabling experimental discrimination via edge-site readout.
